title: Spike Notes — Rollout Controller consuming SLO monitors (latency/error) for auto-rollback
content:
Owner: Benji (Control Plane)
Date range: Jan 16 – Feb 3, 2025
Purpose: feasibility + initial implementation approach for rollout-controller to consume existing latency/error SLO monitors and produce a “verdict” signal used by auto-rollback.

---

1) What we’re trying to prove in this spike
- Can rollout-controller reliably query (or otherwise consume) latency + error SLO signals at the right granularity (route/model/region/tier) with acceptable freshness?
- Can we do this without blowing up observability costs / cardinality / query load?
- Can we keep behavior safe under partial outages (monitor API down, stale data) and avoid noisy rollbacks on low-traffic canaries?

Non-goal for spike: final policy semantics (burn-rate vs fixed threshold) — we only need enough to validate monitor consumption + caching + failure modes.

---

2) Existing monitoring surfaces (what we found)
We have two primary ways to fetch “SLO health” today:

A) Telemetry Query Service (TQS) — query-by-template
- What it gives: raw time series / aggregated metrics over a time range (p50/p95/p99 latency, 5xx rate, request count) for a given label filter.
- Pros:
  - Most flexible; can express exactly what policy engine needs.
  - Lets us compute “must be worse than baseline” comparisons ourselves.
- Cons:
  - More query load; more room for subtle inconsistencies.
  - Higher risk of accidental cardinality explosion if labels aren’t normalized.

B) SLO API (“SLO Summary” endpoint) — monitor-by-id
- What it gives: precomputed SLO status + burn-rate style outputs for a defined SLO object.
- Pros:
  - Cleaner semantics; pushes computation onto observability side.
  - Lower query complexity in rollout-controller.
- Cons:
  - Requires that SLO objects exist for each identity (route/model/region/tier), plus migration work.
  - Harder to do baseline comparison (needs a paired baseline monitor or extra queries).

Spike conclusion: both paths work, but the “monitor-by-id” model will be simplest and safer long-term if we can standardize identity + ensure monitors exist. For initial rollout and during migration, we likely need a hybrid (monitor-by-id when present, fallback to template queries when missing).

---

3) Monitor identity feasibility
We sanity-checked whether our metrics have consistent labels to support an identity contract (route/model/region/tier) and found:
- route: mostly present as route_id; a few services still use route_name or omit route_id in older pipelines.
- model: present as model_id; canary traffic sometimes tagged with model_version but not always with stable “model_id + model_version”.
- region: present as pop/region; naming varies (us-east-1 vs use1 vs iad). We need normalization.
- tier: present for hosted and dedicated; private/on-prem has a different notion (“deployment_id” / “customer_env”). Tier may need to be derived.

Action noted during spike: metric label gaps will block “monitor-by-id” if identity isn’t stable. We should treat label normalization/migration as a dependency (see INT-3310 and upcoming migration workstream).

---

4) API options evaluated (for rollout-controller)
Option 1: Directly query TQS from rollout-controller
- Implementation: add a small client in rollout-controller to call TQS with query templates.
- Data returned: aggregates over window (e.g., p95 latency over last 5m, error rate over last 5m, req count).
- Required: query template library + label normalization helpers.
- Risks: query load, complexity, and subtle “policy computed in controller” drift.

Option 2: “Monitor Registry” + SLO Summary API
- Implementation: controller looks up monitor IDs for (route, model, region, tier) and fetches SLO status (ok/breaching/unknown) and supporting numeric fields.
- Required: a registry mapping identity -> monitor_id; or a deterministic naming convention to discover monitors.
- Risks: registry availability, migration timeline.

Option 3: Push-based event stream from observability (“breach events”)
- Implementation: monitors emit breach events to event bus; controller subscribes.
- Pros: low query load; near real-time.
- Cons: adds new moving parts; exactly-once/idempotency issues; operationally heavy for first version.

Spike recommendation:
- v0: Option 2 with caching, plus Option 1 fallback if monitor_id missing (gated behind feature flag). Do not do push-based in the first milestone.

---

5) Caching strategy (proposed)
Constraints:
- Controller evaluates rollouts frequently (every ~30s to 2m depending on rollout phase).
- We may have many simultaneous rollouts, but we must prevent thundering herd on observability.

Proposed caching layers:

Layer A — Monitor identity -> monitor_id cache
- Key: (route_id, model_id, model_version, region, tier)
- TTL: 30 minutes (monitor IDs don’t change often)
- Negative caching: yes (if not found, cache “miss” for 5 minutes to avoid repeated lookups)

Layer B — Monitor data cache (SLO summary / aggregate results)
- Key: monitor_id + window + query_type (latency/error)
- TTL: 20–30 seconds (accept some staleness; rollback does not need sub-second)
- Stale-while-revalidate: yes (serve cached value if refresh fails, but mark verdict “unknown” if data age > max_staleness)

Layer C — Policy evaluation result cache (verdict)
- Key: rollout_id + policy_id
- TTL: 10 seconds (primarily to dedupe repeated UI polling / event emission)

Additional guardrails:
- Jitter cache refresh to spread load.
- Cap concurrent outbound requests per controller instance (e.g., max 20 inflight) and per-tenant limit (see rate limiting below).

---

6) Rate limits / load estimates
Back-of-envelope:
- Worst case (no caching): N rollouts * 2 metrics (latency/error) * 1–3 windows * evaluation frequency.
  - Example: 200 concurrent rollouts, evaluate every 30s, 2 metrics, 2 windows => ~200 * 4 / 30s ~ 26 qps sustained. Across regions this can multiply.
- With caching (TTL 30s), per controller instance qps drops materially, but a fleet restart could spike.

Proposed rate limiting:
- Per controller instance: token bucket, 50 qps burst / 10 qps sustained to observability APIs.
- Per tenant: cap evaluation queries to 1 qps sustained (burst 5 qps) to avoid a single tenant with many routes causing global load.
- Global rollback guardrail (separate from observability load): limit auto-rollbacks to X per minute per region to avoid cascading rollbacks during shared incidents.

Observability feedback (Nadia/Allison):
- TQS has stricter cost per query than SLO Summary; prefer SLO Summary where possible.
- Any controller-side template querying must ship with a curated template list (no free-form queries) to prevent accidental expensive queries.

---

7) Handling staleness, gaps, and outages (early thinking)
We tested scenarios where monitor data is missing/stale and evaluated desired behavior:

Definitions used in prototype:
- data_age = now - monitor_summary.timestamp
- max_staleness = 2m (tentative)
- warmup_grace = 3–5m from rollout start (configurable)
- min_requests = 100 requests in evaluation window (configurable)

Proposed verdict rules:
- If within warmup_grace OR req_count < min_requests => verdict = “insufficient_data” (should not rollback)
- If monitor fetch fails (timeout/5xx) OR data_age > max_staleness => verdict = “unknown”
- If unknown: default policy should be fail-open for rollback (do not rollback) but emit alert/event so humans know auto-rollback is blind.
  - Rationale: monitoring outages should not trigger rollback loops.

Open question: Some enterprise tenants asked for fail-closed semantics (treat unknown as breach) in regulated environments. Needs explicit per-tenant config + very careful rollout.

---

8) Prototype implementation notes (what we built)
Prototype branch (not merged) in rollout-controller:
- Implemented a basic “SLOMonitorClient”:
  - fetchMonitorId(identity)
  - fetchSloSummary(monitorId, window)
- Local in-memory cache (LRU) for both ID and data.
- Implemented a tiny “decision trace” object for debugging:
  - identity, monitor_id, window, observed values, data_age, req_count, result
- Wired to a dummy policy evaluator that compares against fixed thresholds.

Local testing:
- Used a staging tenant with a canary model rollout and forced a latency regression by reducing batch size.
- Observed:
  - Summary fetch latency: p50 ~80–120ms, p95 ~250–400ms (staging)
  - Occasional 1–2s tail when observability busy
  - Cache effectiveness: ~85–95% hit rate after the first minute

Important: “monitor summary timestamp” is not always aligned with query time; some summaries update on 30–60s cadence. This means even if we evaluate every 10s, new data may not exist.

Conclusion: evaluation frequency < 30s doesn’t buy much, and increases load. Recommend evaluating every 30s or 60s depending on rollout phase.

---

9) Query/window shapes that seemed to work
For both latency and error we tried:
- short window: 2m or 5m (fast detection)
- long window: 10m or 15m (stability / reduce flapping)

Early result:
- 5m window with min_requests gate produced much less noise than 2m.
- For error spikes, 2m was useful but only for sufficiently high traffic.

Tentative default suggestion (subject to ADR 0148):
- error: evaluate 2m AND 10m (require breach in both, or use burn-rate semantics)
- latency: evaluate 5m AND 15m

We also tested “must be worse than baseline” concept:
- Baseline candidate: previous stable version of same model/route/region/tier.
- Feasibility: works if we can reliably fetch baseline monitor for prior version.
- Challenge: baseline monitor identity must include model_version. If baseline version is not receiving enough traffic (e.g., canary moved most traffic), baseline becomes insufficient_data.

---

10) Key risks surfaced
- Label normalization is the largest practical risk. If identity labels aren’t consistent, we’ll be stuck in template-query mode, which increases load and complexity.
- Low-traffic routes: without min_requests gating, we get false positives on latency percentiles (unstable stats).
- Monitor cadence: SLO summary values may lag by 30–60s; rollback speed expectations should factor that in.
- Fleet restart / deploy: cold caches can create spikes to observability. Need jitter + rate limits + possibly shared cache (Redis) if it becomes a problem.
- Multi-tenant incident: If a shared dependency causes broad SLO breaches, auto-rollback could attempt to roll back many rollouts simultaneously. Executor needs per-tenant throttling + global safety limits.

---

11) Recommendations / next steps
Recommended path to unblock ENG-2312:
1) Implement MonitorClient in rollout-controller with:
   - strict allowlist of endpoints (no arbitrary queries)
   - caching layers (identity -> monitor_id, monitor_id -> summary)
   - timeouts + retries with exponential backoff
   - explicit “unknown” + “insufficient_data” verdict propagation
2) Coordinate with observability team to confirm:
   - expected SLO summary update cadence
   - supported QPS limits per client
   - fields available for request counts and timestamp freshness
3) Define the minimum viable monitor identity contract (ADR 0147) and start label normalization backlog for missing labels.

Open questions to resolve before production rollout:
- Do we store monitor_id in rollout config at rollout creation time, or always resolve by identity at evaluation time?
  - Storing reduces runtime dependency but can become stale if monitors are re-created.
- Do we require both latency + error monitors for auto-rollback to be enabled, or allow partial coverage?
- What should be the exact max_staleness threshold and escalation path if unknown persists > X minutes?
- Is there any customer data segregation requirement that prevents controller from querying shared observability endpoints for Dedicated/Private?

---

12) Appendix: notes from quick stakeholder pings
- Allison (Observability): prefer monitor-by-id; will help define stable identity tags; strongly against controller-side arbitrary queries.
- Nadia (Telemetry): label normalization work is ongoing; can add translation for region naming (use1/us-east-1) in the query layer as an interim fix.
- Miles (SRE): insist on “unknown” verdict behavior + alerting; do not rollback on unknown. Also wants a simple way to pause auto-rollback per rollout.
- Rafael (Oncall): runbook should include verifying monitor freshness (timestamp) and how to distinguish “unknown due to monitor outage” from “no traffic.”

End of notes.
